# Relationship Between AI Literacy and AI-TPACK

## Servet Üztemur, PhD1 [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-1580-9123) Görkem Avcı, PhD2, Ali Gökalp, PhD3 [,](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-3301-8392) and Nail Değirmenci4

## Abstract

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education holds significant potential to develop innovative and inclusive learning environments. This study investigated the relationship between teachers’ AI literacy and their AI-TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge integrated with AI). It further explored the mediating role of innovative thinking and the moderating effect of AI anxiety within this relationship. The research was conducted with 378 Turkish teachers (50.8% female). Findings demonstrated statistically significant positive relationships among AI literacy, AI-TPACK, and innovative thinking. Conversely, AI anxiety was negatively correlated with the other variables. Moreover, innovative thinking was found to significantly mediate the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK. Additionally, AI anxiety moderates the AI literacy-AI-TPACK relationship; specifically, this relationship strengthens as teachers’ AI anxiety diminishes. The results underscore the critical importance of promoting innovative thinking and reducing AI anxiety to empower teachers to integrate AI effectively in education.

## Keywords

### AI anxiety, innovative thinking, teachers’ AI literacy, AI-TPACK, moderated mediation analysis

improving teachers’ competencies and providing students with inclusive, personalized, and immersive experiences (Algerafi et al., 2023). The ubiquity of AI, including in the classroom, makes it essential for teachers to use and understand this technology (Kasinidou et al., 2025). Therefore, identifying which skills, approaches, and barriers are practical for teachers to integrate AI into educational processes is important. Teachers are responsible for educating the next generation about AI. Conversely, awareness of their concerns about AI can accelerate adaptation by addressing potential issues. On the other hand, innovative thinking tendencies can enrich learning environments with different AI applications. Therefore, by combining these variables, teachers, as role models, convey information, promote trust and motivation, and empower students to meaningfully interact with and become competent with new technologies such as AI (Felix, 2020). To improve AI literacy and core digital competences, schools, teachers, and students must adjust to the shift toward a digital society (Šorgo, 2017). Teachers’ integration of advanced AI technologies into education to keep their teaching-learning activities up-to-date requires competence in AI literacy (Ding et al., 2024). Today, teachers’ AI literacy is crucial for several reasons, including personalized learning, professional development, innovation, ethics, and safety awareness (Younis, 2025). Teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge about AI (AI-TPACK) is another crucial factor for AI literacy. Nevertheless, teachers’ viewpoints, convictions, and opinions profoundly affect the understanding and operationalization of the curriculum (Velander et al., 2024). Equipping teachers with pedagogically sound strategies and skills is crucial for effectively integrating AI into complex educational contexts (Ding et al., 2024; Gökalp & Değirmenci, 2025). When teachers possess adequate AI-TPACK to use AI-based tools, AI technology becomes available for effective teaching (Cavalcanti et al., 2021).

The contributions of AI to learning environments can revolutionize education and teaching paradigms, including the need to improve educators’ information and skills. Teachers, as central actors in the education system, need to develop their competencies and attitudes towards technology to make the most efficient use of AI in teaching in the current technological era. This development is the foundation for effectively incorporating AI into education (Polak et al., 2022). Cultivating this skill in the educational sector requires innovative thinking, familiarity with new methods, techniques, and strategies, as well as fresh perspectives (Bueno et al., 2023). An understanding of education that fulfills the requirements of the age, is open to innovation, and seeks to lead innovation will benefit both the teacher and the students.

### _1.1. AI Literacy and AI-TPACK_

With the transformation brought about by the digital age, AI literacy and AI TPACK are changing educational paradigms by enabling teachers to understand AI technologies and adapt their pedagogical strategies accordingly. Therefore, given AI’s increasing presence and impact in education (Sperling et al., 2024), different explanations of AI literacy have been developed. To explain AI literacy in the academic context, Ng et al. (2021) introduced a framework with four dimensions: knowing and understanding AI, implementing AI applications, creating and evaluating AI applications, and ethical issues. First, knowing and understanding AI is fundamental, as teachers must have a basic grasp of AI concepts and familiarity with advanced AI applications (Cantú-Ortiz, 2020). Integrating AI into educational contexts necessitates progressing from theoretical comprehension to applied pedagogical strategies. When going beyond basic knowledge of artificial intelligence (AI), the application of AI-focused methodologies becomes critical for optimizing teaching practices and increasing professional effectiveness. Concurrently, the expanding role of AI in education underscores the need for a systematic evaluation of its pedagogical utility, including empirical assessments of its instructional relevance, impact on learning outcomes, and alignment with curricular objectives (Shi & Choi, 2024). Furthermore, ethical considerations must remain central to AI adoption, requiring educators to critically examine its deployment through institutional ethics, societal values, and equity frameworks. This involves addressing challenges such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, equitable access to AI tools, and the sociotechnical consequences of AI-driven decision-making in educational ecosystems (Latif et al., 2023). AI is progressively recognized as a transformative force in education, offering numerous benefits for classroom education (Younis, 2025). AI literacy has recently become a focus in education and has raised expectations for teachers’ and teacher educators’ professional knowledge (Sperling et al., 2024). AI literacy can be developed in individuals through educational activities that incorporate practical strategies, methods, and techniques. AI literacy has become a crucial aspect of digital literacy, reshaping the ways people communicate, work, learn, and live (Long & Magerko, 2020). It has become a core 21st- century digital literacy skill connected to key competencies like problem-solving and collaboration, and the use of technology for social good. On the other hand, AI literacy is not only about the ability to apply and comprehend AI-related concepts, but also about becoming a problem solver capable of effectively applying AI concepts to real-world problems (Ng et al., 2023). Advancing AI literacy is increasingly crucial for individuals to understand how AI functions, its potential societal impacts, and how to approach it responsibly, considering ethical and safety concerns (Ng & Chu, 2021). AI in education refers to the use of AI technology to improve learning and teaching in schools (Chen et al., 2020). It utilizes AI-powered portals, platforms, and tools to customize learning experiences, track student progress, provide instructor 

_Üztemur et al._ 3 

feedback, and automate repetitive management tasks. With the growing incorporation of AI applications in education, a fundamental question arises regarding the effectiveness of the TPACK framework in addressing teachers’ current in- structional practices and professional growth needs (Sofyan et al., 2023). This inquiry examines whether the TPACK model needs to be transformed or include new elements in the age of AI. Integrating AI technology within the TPACK framework has revolutionary potential to change teaching practices, learning environments, and other learning and training activities (Elmaadaway & Abouelenein, 2023). Hence, building an AI-based TPACK model (AI-TPACK) is emerging as a promising field of study and investigation. The new model will integrate the existing aspects of TPACK and be embedded with artificial intelligence to facilitate more effective and creative pedagogical approaches that keep pace with the fast-evolving AI in education. AI-TPACK research is crucial for gaining insight into how AI can improve pedagogy and support instructors in adapting to the rapid digital transformation (Celik, 2023).

TPACK is recognized as an adaptable model for diverse technological tools, teaching methods, and instructional strategies (Valtonen et al., 2017). In AI education, this framework has been extended to include AI technology, referred to as AI-TPACK, which comprises the integration of content, pedagogical, and AI technological knowledge (Reyes Jr et al., 2017). This model is a specialized method for teaching specific disciplines using AI technology, equipping educators to deliver lessons efficiently and effectively ([Adipat, 2021)](#5-conclusion). In this era where AI goes beyond its conventional function as a tool, it is essential to equip teachers with the necessary skills. This emphasizes the crucial role of AI in the teaching-learning experience. Unlike traditional information technologies, AI literacy permeates and impacts teaching and learning across all dimensions, transforming educators’ cognitive frameworks and instructional practices (Vieriu & Petrea, 2025). This viewpoint emphasizes the necessity of incorporating AI technology not merely as an additional resource but as an essential part of the educational process, transforming the presentation and comprehension of educational content in the era of AI (Ning et al., 2024).

### _1.2. The Mediating Role of Innovative Thinking in the Relationship Between AI Literacy and AI-TPACK_

While innovative thinking is widely recognized, its explanation has often been limited (Barak et al., 2013). Innovative thinking involves creating solutions that benefit society or enhance welfare. The development of innovative thinking relies on the ability to analyze context, create concepts, collaborate, reflect, represent, and evaluate situations in the present tense (Wu et al., 2013). The concept of innovative thinking is prominent at various educational levels. Innovative thinking generates new ideas in learning environments in response to children’s educational needs (Hart, 1996). From an educational standpoint, it signifies a cognitive process that serves as a foundation for implementing significantly improved or completely new ideas (Barak et al., 2013). During the past decade, technology has significantly changed education in many facets of learning by improving access to learning materials and extending higher education beyond traditional classroom settings, thereby creating new opportunities for students and educators (Celik, 2023). AI technologies have the capacity to revolutionize all areas of life, including education. By shaping education and training, AI facilitates changes in educators’ cognitive structures and teaching methodologies that depart from traditional knowledge approaches (Long & Magerko, 2020). With AI’s rapid advancement and integration into our lives, digital skills have expanded to encompass AI literacy (Carlisle et al., 2023). For educators to respond effectively to the demands of the AI era, the TPACK framework must adopt new approaches that align with contemporary trends (Sun et al., 2023). TPACK is a widely recognized model for assessing teachers’ competencies in using technology for teaching and learning, highlighting their capabilities regarding teaching methods for specific curriculum topics (Malik et al., 2019; Zimmermann et al., 2021). Especially in light of the emergence of generative AI, it has become urgent to reconsider the relationships among technology, pedagogy, and content knowledge and to create a new AI-TPACK framework for the AI era. Interest in the use of AI in education is increasing, and it is considered capable of completely revolutionizing how learning and teaching occur (Cooper, 2023; Doğan et al., 2023; Rawas, 2024). AI-based tools offer pedagogical opportunities, including personalized instruction, increased student engagement, and improved educational efficiency (Luan et al., 2020). For teachers, AI can facilitate the evaluation of students’ advanced understanding (Chen et al., 2021), help assess the instructional process, and assist in course planning (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). Integrating AI into instructional methods is essential to equip students for a future dominated by technology (Ding et al., 2024). Teachers’ AI literacy is important for AI-TPACK, which encompasses AI-integrated technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge. Therefore, it is crucial to provide teachers with pedagogically sound strategies and skills to integrate AI effectively and efficiently in complex educational contexts (Ding et al., 2024). When teachers possess sufficient AI-TPACK knowledge, they can effectively employ AI-powered tools (Cavalcanti et al., 2021). Enhancing teachers’ knowledge of AI increases the potential to foster student motivation and engagement, enabling them to use AI-powered tools for personalized learning and prompt feedback (Popenici & Kerr, 2017; Wang et al., 2021). The role of TPACK in integrating technology into education is undeniable (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Teachers have a vital role in preparing students as 21st-century citizens (Klaeijsen et al., 2018). They must possess innovative thinking skills and be able to follow and experience the innovations of the age (Suryawati & Osman, 2017). Innovative thinking has a critical unifying role in enhancing educators’ capacity to implement AI-TPACK effectively. As education systems evolve, it becomes imperative to encourage innovative thinking among educators to maximize the pedagogical potential of AI and develop adaptive, future-ready teaching practices. To provide meaningful educational experiences, professional development programmes must prioritize AI competence and innovative pedagogical strategies.

### _1.3. Moderator Role of AI Anxiety_

AI has emerged as a fundamental component in daily life. This affects everyone, including young children who are not competent in using AI tools. Despite AI’s widespread presence, many users remain unaware of its integration into these technologies and the ethical considerations arising from its use (Long et al., 2021). It is precisely at this point that people experience varying levels of anxiety and ethical concerns about the future of AI as they become aware of its increasing prevalence and impact ([Ahmad et al., 2023;](#5-conclusion) Lin et al., 2025; Rashid & Kausik, 2024). AI anxiety is defined as an emotional fear arising from concern that technological tools may threaten the essence of being ‘human’ and prevent individuals from interacting with AI (Wang & Wang, 2019). AI anxiety refers to feelings of fear and apprehension related to AI, often perceived as uncontrollable.

There is a perception that AI poses a threat to humanity, particularly in terms of human occupations. Many users express concerns about becoming unemployed and see AI as a potential disruptor in various professional fields (Shoufan, 2023). Although computerization and automation will inevitably replace some human work, teachers still play a leading role in education. However, teachers and other education-related actors must adapt and accommodate AI technologies and products to prepare for such AI educational developments. (Terzi, 2020). Teachers are crucial in transferring understanding of AI and cultivating their students’ AI literacy (Kasinidou et al., 2025). Despite this, teachers are concerned about their limited un- derstanding of AI and technical skills, which limits their ability to utilize AI educational practices effectively. They are also concerned about using AI to effectively teach regarding AI and incorporate AI within their instructional methods (Ng et al., 2023). Modern educators should lead students in leveraging technology to enhance their learning experiences (Jin & Schmidt- Crawford, 2022). Nevertheless, AI’s potential remains underutilized in education (Luckin et al., 2022). Therefore, using AI in teaching environments lags behind other sectors (Luckin & Cukurova, 2019). One contributing factor is that, to date, the role of teachers in integrating AI-based tools into education has been neglected (Seufert et al., 2021). Teachers’ technological and pedagogical knowledge of AI is crucial for effectively incorporating AI into education. Moreover, because of new moral concerns raised by AI, teachers must possess the knowledge to evaluate AI-based decisions (Celik, 2023). Despite the benefits of AI-based tools, ethical concerns pose significant challenges to their application in education (Castelvecchi, 2016). For example, AI may increase inequality among students’ socio-economic variables (gender, parental education level, etc.) (Shin, 2020). Therefore, AI anxiety is a concept that defines teachers’ concerns about AI technologies and their feelings of insecurity and uncertainty (Liu & Liu, 2025). However, teachers’ anxiety on this issue can significantly impact the transformation of AI literacy into creative thinking and, consequently, the development of AI-TPACK competencies. While low AI anxiety allows teachers to comfortably and innovatively apply their AI skills in the classroom, high levels of anxiety can negatively affect technology integration in education by increasing concerns, resistance, and reluctance towards AI (Henderson & Corry, 2021). The AI-TPACK model provides an important insight into how to maximize the link between emotional barriers, such as anxiety level, and technological competence in teachers’ professional development activities. From this perspective, the moderating function of AI anxiety is a key factor in helping teachers translate the knowledge and skills gained through AI literacy into creative thinking and to apply practical, efficient AI-related teaching methods in the field of AI-TPACK (Schiavo et al., 2024). The model provides important understandings of enhancing the sustainability of teachers’ adoption of AI and their adaptation processes in the digital age.

### _1.4. Current Study_

AI literacy enables teachers to distinguish more effectively which tools are compatible with specific pedagogical goals when applying AI tools within the framework of intelligent TPACK, with an understanding grounded in AI principles, thus making the application more purposeful and effective (Kong et al., 2022; Velander et al., 2024). AI literacy was identified to have a positive predictive influence on AI-TPACK. In this context, [Al-Abdullatif (2024)](#5-conclusion) found that AI literacy has a positive predictive effect on TPACK, further emphasizing its role in equipping educators with the essential skills and understanding needed to incorporate the researcher-developed GenAI tool into their teaching effectively. AI can free teachers from tedious administrative and teaching tasks, enabling them to concentrate on innovative endeavors (Bodén, 2023). However, ethical issues (transparency, equity, inclusiveness, and fairness) raise significant concerns about the use of AI in education (Shin, 2020). Concerns and anxieties about AI play a vital role in the adoption of AI technology. Since AI anxiety is negatively correlated with perceived benefit, educators with AI anxiety may be skeptical of AI-generated content, which could reduce 

_Üztemur et al._ 5 

their perception of the tool’s utility (Pan et al., 2025). However, emphasizing that studies examining the relationships among AI literacy, AI acceptance, and AI anxiety remain scarce, Schiavo et al. (2024) found that AI literacy positively predicted AI acceptance and negatively predicted AI anxiety. Similarly, Cengiz and Peker (2025), who found a negative correlation between AI literacy and AI anxiety, emphasized that university students’ knowledge of AI is crucial for reducing their anxiety about AI. It is also noted that the correlation between teachers’ AI-TPACK levels and AI literacy warrants further exploration (Ning et al., 2024). This study investigated the relationship between teachers’ AI literacy and their AI-TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge integrated with AI). It further explored the mediating role of innovative thinking and the moderating effect of AI anxiety within this relationship. Thus, the present study uniquely addresses a gap in the existing literature by investigating the mediating role of innovative thinking and the moderating effect of AI anxiety on the relationship between teachers’ AI literacy and AI-TPACK. The following hypotheses were tested.

**(H1)**. AI literacy positively predicts innovative thinking. **(H2)**. Innovative thinking positively predicts AI-TPACK.

**(H3)**. Innovative thinking mediates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK. **(H4)**. AI anxiety moderates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK.

Based on the conceptual framework outlined above and the literature, the model in [Figure 1](#2-method) was proposed, and the hypotheses above were tested in line with it.

## 2. Method

### _2.1. Participants and Procedure_

This study was conducted with 378 Turkish teachers (Female = 50.8%, Age(mean): 38.17) aged between 22 and 58 years, whose characteristics are presented in [Table 1.](#22-measures) Data were collected online via WhatsApp using Google Forms between November 2024 and February 2025. Teachers were recruited using convenience sampling. The necessary ethics committee approvals were obtained prior to the study, and the procedures were designed in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Teachers were assured that their personal information would be kept confidential and would not be shared with third parties. All teachers provided e-informed consent before participating in the online survey and answered the questions anonymously. The instructions emphasized that there were no right or wrong answers and that each answer reflected the teachers’ views and beliefs. Teachers did not receive any payment. No missing data was found as all items in the questionnaire were required to be answered.

### _2.2. Measures_

The research data were collected using four different scales: Intelligent-TPACK Scale (AI-TPACK), Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS), Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS), and Innovative Thinking Tendency Scale (ITTS). The language and form validity of AIAS and AILS, adapted to Turkish culture with the support of experts who are fluent in both English and Turkish, was ensured through pilot applications ([Akkaya et al., 2021;](#5-conclusion) Çelebi et al., 2023). The validity of the scales in the current research sample was tested by Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA). The fit index values recommended by Byrne (2016) were considered (χ2/df \[≤5\], RMSEA \[≤.08\], SRMR \[≤.08\], CFI \[≥.90\], and TLI \[≥.90\]). For reliability, McDonald’s (ω) and Cronbach’s alpha (α) internal consistency coefficients were calculated. According to George and Mallery (2010), the internal consistency coefficient value is expected to be ≥ 0.70. See [Table 2](#22-measures) for the fit indices and calculated internal consistency coefficients for the scales.

#### _2.2.1. Intelligent–TPACK Scale (AI-TPACK)_

AI-TPACK is a tool designed to extend the TPACK framework, which includes teachers’ technological, pedagogical, and content knowledge, with ethical dimensions (Celik, 2023). AI-TPACK consists of 27 items and five sub-dimensions (Intelligent TPK, Intelligent TPACK, Intelligent TK, Intelligent TCK, and Ethics). AI-TPACK has a 7-point Likert-type measurement with options ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

#### _2.2.2. Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS)_

AIAS was used to assess teachers’ AI anxiety levels (Wang & Wang, 2019; Turkish adaptation = [Akkaya et al., 2021)](#5-conclusion). The AIAS has 16 items and four subscales (Learning, Job Replacement, Sociotechnical Blindness, and AI Config- uration). The AIAS has a 7-point Likert-type measurement, with options ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

#### _2.2.3. Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale (AILS)_

The AILS, originally developed by Wang et al. (2022) and adapted into Turkish by Çelebi et al. (2023), was used to assess teachers’ AI literacy levels. The scale comprises four sub-dimensions (Usage, Evaluation, Awareness, and Ethics), each represented by three items. It uses a 7-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating greater AI literacy.

#### _2.2.4. Innovative Thinking Tendency Scale (ITTS)_

The ITTS, developed by Bilir et al. (2023), is a unidimensional tool comprising 10 items that assesses teachers’ inclination toward innovative thinking. It employs a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating a greater tendency toward innovative thought.

For all measures, items were coded so that higher scores reflect higher levels of the construct, including greater AI literacy, higher AI-TPACK, stronger innovative thinking, and increased AI anxiety.

### _2.3. Statistical Analysis_

#### _2.3.1. Preliminary Analysis_

Descriptive statistics and correlation analyses were applied in preliminary analyses. Pearson product-moment correlation coefficients were used to examine the relationships between the study variables (AI literacy, innovative thinking, AI anxiety, and AI-TPACK). Jeffreys’s Amazing Statistics Program (JASP) version 0.19.2 was used for CFA. IBM SPSS version 25 was used for all other analyses. Statistical significance was defined as a p-value \< 0.05.

#### _2.3.2. Conditional Process Analysis_

SPSS PROCESS macro Model 5, developed by Hayes (2022), was used in moderated mediation analyses. SPSS PROCESS macro Model 5 allows for analyses of both mediating and moderating effects (Hayes, 2022). For this reason, this model was chosen to examine whether AI literacy has an indirect effect on AI-TPACK through innovative thinking and also to assess the moderating effect of AI anxiety on the link between AI literacy and AI-TPACK.

In the model, the path shown in [Figure 1,](#2-method) with innovative thinking as the dependent variable and AI literacy as the independent variable, was tested. Then, the model in which AI-TPACK is the dependent variable is established. Here, the significance of the effect of innovative thinking on AI-TPACK (path b) and the indirect effect coefficient of AI literacy on AI- TPACK (path c1 \[a\*b\]) was examined. To assess whether the indirect effect coefficient is significant, it is tested using 5000 bootstrap samples, with a 95% confidence interval, as suggested by Hayes (2022). Significant effects are supported when the confidence interval for the difference between the lower (LL) and upper (UL) limits does not contain zero (Hayes, 2022). To assess the moderating effect of AI anxiety, the interaction effect of the independent variable and the moderator variable (AI literacy x AI anxiety), i.e., the c3 path, was tested for significance (Hayes, 2022). The “-1SD, Mean, +1SD” feature was chosen and offered by PROCESS to determine the low, medium, and high levels of AI anxiety.

## 3. Results

### _3.1. Preliminary Analyses_

[Table 3](#222-artificial-intelligence-anxiety-scale-aias) presents correlation values and descriptive statistics for the relevant variables. As can be seen from the kurtosis and skewness values in [Table 3,](#222-artificial-intelligence-anxiety-scale-aias) the variables were normally distributed (kurtosis and skewness ±1; Kline, 2015). There were statistically significant positive correlations between AI literacy, innovative thinking, and AI-TPACK. AI anxiety has statistically significant negative relationships with all variables.

### _3.2. Moderated Mediation Analyses_

[Table 4](#3-results) presents the unstandardized beta coefficients for the moderated mediation effect of AI literacy on AI-TPACK. When[ Table 4](#3-results) [i](#3-results)s examined, the direct effect of AI literacy on innovative thinking was positive and statistically significant (b = .20, SE = .02, p \< .001; 95% CI \[.15, .25\]). The model was statistically significant (F(1, 376) = 64.40, p \< .001), AI literacy explained 14.6% of the variance in innovative thinking (R2 = .146), and hypothesis H1 was confirmed. In the model where AI-TPACK was the dependent variable, the effect of AI literacy on AI-TPACK was positive and statistically significant (b = .61, SE = .04, p \< .001; 95% CI \[.52, .69\]). Moreover, the effect of innovative thinking on AI-TPACK was positive and statistically significant (b = .44, SE = .08, p \< .001; 95% CI \[.27, .60\]), thereby confirming H2. The indirect effect of AI literacy on AI-TPACK through innovative thinking was estimated using 5,000 bootstrap samples. The analysis revealed a positive indirect effect (b = .09, SE = .01), and the 95% percentile bootstrap CI did not contain zero (\[.05, .12\]). These results indicate that innovative thinking mediates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK, supporting Hypothesis H3.

The effect of AI anxiety on AI-TPACK was statistically nonsignificant (_b_ = -.04, _SE_ = .03, _p_ \> .05; 95% \[-.10, .03\]). On the other hand, the effect of the interaction variable (AI literacy × AI anxiety) on AI-TPACK was statistically significant (_b_ = -.10, _SE_ = .02, _p_ \< .001; 95% CI \[-.15, -.050\]). The model was statistically significant (_F_(4, 373) = 91.27, _p_ \< .001), and the independent, mediator, and moderator variables explained 49.4% of the variance in AI-TPACK (_R2_ = .494). These findings confirm hypothesis H4.

According to[ Table 4,](#3-results) for the conditional effects of AI literacy according to whether the moderator variable is -1SD, Mean, and +1SD, the effect of -1SD (b = .76, SE = .05, t = 13.16, p \< .001; 95% CI \[.64, .87\]), the effect of mean (b = .61, SE = .04, t = 13.85, p \< .001; 95% \[.52, .70\]), and the effect of +1SD (b = .46, SE = .05, t = 7.72, p \< .001; 95% CI \[.34, .58\]) were statistically significant. The results of simple slopes analyses examining how the conditional effects of AI literacy on AI- TPACK vary across moderator values are visualized in [Figure 2.](#4-discussion)

According to [Figure 2,](#4-discussion) as AI literacy increases across all three AI anxiety groups, the average AI-TPACK scores also increase. This shows that AI anxiety modulates the relationship between teachers’ AI literacy and AI-TPACK, and this relationship strengthens as teachers’ AI anxiety decreases. The change in R2 resulting from this interaction was statistically significant (_F_(1, 373) = 14.7366, _p_ \< .01), and its contribution to the explained variance was _ΔR2_ = .020. ## 4. Discussion

This study examined a conditional process model linking Turkish teachers’ AI literacy to AI-TPACK, with innovative thinking serving as a mediator and AI anxiety functioning as a moderator. The findings demonstrate that AI literacy positively predicts AI-TPACK and that innovative thinking accounts for a significant portion of this effect, supporting the view that teachers translate AI-related knowledge into stronger AI-integrated pedagogical skills, in part through a more innovation- focused mindset. Additionally, AI anxiety significantly moderated the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK, such that the positive link was stronger at lower levels of AI anxiety, indicating that emotional barriers can weaken how teachers translate AI literacy into AI-TPACK in practice. The present findings corroborate previous studies suggesting that AI literacy and AI-TPACK are positively associated. Teachers who understand AI principles can use AI tools more purposefully and effectively in alignment with pedagogical goals within the AI-TPACK framework (Kong et al., 2022; Velander et al., 2024). Increasing teachers’ AI literacy may also help reduce barriers arising from limited understanding and experience with AI tools and may strengthen their competencies in AI integration (Kim & Kwon, 2023). To succeed in the ever-evolving AI- focused educational environment, this competency enables both the selection of appropriate teaching strategies and consideration of ethical issues (Cantú-Ortiz et al., 2020). AI-TPACK expands the foundational TPACK framework to include AI technology (Reyes Jr et al., 2017). Content, pedagogical, and artificial intelligence technological knowledge intersect to form AI-TPACK (Celik, 2023). AI literacy is a prerequisite for enriching the technological dimension of TPACK ([Al-Abdullatif, 2024;](#5-conclusion) Laupichler et al., 2022). The current research findings demonstrated that AI literacy has a positive predictive impact on AI-TPACK. The results support [Al-Abdullatif’s (2024)](#5-conclusion) conclusions. It plays a key role in equipping teachers with the knowledge and skills they need to successfully incorporate GenAI and AI tools into their lessons. Importantly, the moderation effect was small in size (ΔR2 = .020), suggesting that AI anxiety adds modest explanatory value while still being theoretically meaningful as an emotional factor that can constrain teachers’ use of AI literacy in developing AI-TPACK.

This study also revealed a positive association between AI literacy and AI-TPACK and innovative thinking. Innovative thinking stands out as an important and integrative element in teachers’ development towards the practical application of AI- TPACK skills. It is also among the findings that innovative thinking mediates the relationship between AI literacy and AI- TPACK. The concept of innovative thinking, prevalent across various levels of education, is a cognitive process that lays the groundwork for putting original or more advanced ideas into practice (Barak et al., 2013). Teachers who integrate technology into their teaching processes and practices are more enthusiastic about these topics and are more courageous in overcoming the challenges they face when implementing innovative ideas (Njiku et al., 2022). Innovative approaches significantly enhance students’ thinking skills (Kwangmuang et al., 2021). The results showed that innovative thinking significantly mediates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK. This situation reveals that merely having knowledge of AI is insufficient for teachers; they need innovative thinking to transform that knowledge into pedagogical practices (Celik, 2023). Innovative thinking can help develop creative and effective teaching strategies by leveraging new technologies, such as AI. As education systems evolve with technology, fostering innovative thinking among educators becomes essential to maximize AI’s pedagogical potential and develop adaptable teaching practices. It was found that concerns and worries about AI were negatively related to teachers’ knowledge, competence, and innovative approaches to AI. This suggests that anxiety indicates a negative association with these factors.

AI literacy can equip educators with a foundational understanding of AI concepts, applications, evaluation processes, and ethical considerations. This competence is defined as a teacher’s ability to recognize and comprehend the potential uses of AI- powered tools (Sperling et al., 2024). However, this knowledge alone may be insufficient for teachers to effectively integrate AI into their pedagogical methods. In this context, innovative thinking enables teachers to transform knowledge gained through AI literacy to align with the dynamic needs and pedagogical goals of the classroom. This process goes beyond mere tool usage, becoming a deliberate and creative synthesis of AI with instructional content and pedagogical approaches (Walter, 2024). Consequently, this serves as a critical foundation for AI-TPACK. Therefore, the mediating role of innovative thinking allows us to interpret the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK not merely as a statistical correlation but as a fundamental cognitive process that empowers teachers to develop dynamic and creative educational practices in response to the demands of the digital age. This underscores the importance of explicitly addressing and fostering innovative thinking within professional development programs for teachers.

Limitations in AI knowledge and concerns about teachers’ technical skills can lead to anxiety when using AI (Ng et al., 2023). The current study showed that the link between AI literacy and AI-TPACK is influenced by AI anxiety and that this relationship strengthens as teachers’ AI anxiety decreases. This finding supports the results of a study by Pan et al. (2025), which show that AI anxiety is negatively associated with perceived usefulness and that anxious educators may approach AI- generated content with skepticism. Moreover, empirical evidence that AI proficiency is a negative predictor of AI-induced anxiety (Schiavo et al., 2024) and that exposure to AI helps alleviate such anxiety (Cengiz & Peker, 2025) corroborates the present study’s findings. Within the scope of this study, it was observed that AI anxiety is an important factor in teachers’ approaches to incorporating AI into their teaching processes and that reducing this anxiety is associated with a more effective transformation of AI literacy into AI-TPACK competences. These findings suggest that low AI anxiety may allow teachers to apply AI skills in the classroom more comfortably and innovatively. While these relationships are challenging to articulate within a direct cause-and-effect framework, given the cross-sectional nature of the study, they suggest a potential role for AI anxiety in this transformation.

From a socio-psychological perspective, teachers’ concerns about AI can be attributed to a combination of factors. First, teachers may feel inadequate due to insufficient knowledge and technical support regarding AI. This situation may reinforce teachers’ perception that their professional identity and roles are threatened by AI (Zhou et al., 2024). In addition, this situation may increase individual anxiety by heightening fears of job loss. On the other hand, rapid technological de- velopments in AI may trigger fears of losing control and being unable to keep up. This situation can cause tension and panic due to uncertainty (McClure, 2018). On the other hand, ethical issues such as algorithmic bias, transparency, and data privacy can increase teachers’ distrust of AI (Kim & Kim, 2022). All of these socio-psychological factors can create conditions that hinder teachers’ ability to incorporate AI into their educational processes. For this reason, practical experiences and supportive interventions that can increase teachers’ AI literacy and alleviate their concerns are crucial for facilitating adaptation to technological change.

### _4.1. Limitations and Directions for Future Research_

The study has some limitations. Firstly, this study used convenience sampling, a non-probability sampling method. The cross-sectional data were collected via Google Forms, and participating teachers were contacted via WhatsApp and email. 

_Üztemur et al._ 11 

This approach, by its nature, limits the sample’s generalizability. The voluntary inclusion of participants via an online survey may have introduced a self-selection effect. It may limit the capacity of the resulting sample to fully represent the broader population of teachers in Turkey. Therefore, caution should be exercised in generalizing the findings to teachers in different cultural or geographical regions. Secondly, the use of a single source and method for data collection introduces the risk of common method bias, which may artificially inflate the observed relationships among variables. To mitigate this risk, respondent anonymity was ensured, clear and comprehensible instructions were provided within the online survey, and the items were presented in a randomized order. Nevertheless, survey-based data inherently carry the possibility of responses influenced by social desirability or subjective perceptions. This tendency may have led teachers to report their self-assessed AI Literacy scores higher than they actually are, while underreporting their AI Anxiety levels. Future research should address this limitation by employing multiple data sources (e.g., observational data or performance metrics in addition to teacher self- reports) or by adopting longitudinal designs to examine relationships among variables more deeply. Lastly, the study has a cross-sectional design. Therefore, it is difficult to make firm causal claims about the relationships between variables, but mediation and moderation analyses have provided important information about their nature. Given the limitations of this study, additional studies with different sample groups (e.g., across countries or education levels) can be conducted. Furthermore, longitudinal studies examining changes over time in the relationships among AI literacy, AI-TPACK, innovative thinking, and AI anxiety, or qualitative studies to gain a deeper understanding of teachers’ experiences, can be conducted. Extending the research’s recommendations towards teacher professional development, policy, and resource development is possible. To improve teachers’ AI literacy and AI-TPACK competencies, professional development programs focused on specific goals should be developed. These programs should go beyond the technical use of AI and encompass its integration into pedagogical practices and ethical considerations (Gökalp & Değirmenci, 2025; Latif et al., 2023; Shin, 2020). Based on these findings, a module can be created to increase AI literacy and AI-TPACK competence in education. This module aims to help teachers understand the basic concepts of AI and develop their ability to integrate AI with pedagogical knowledge. In terms of content, the basic concepts of AI, its types (e.g., machine learning, natural language processing), and its potential in education can be addressed. In addition, the AI-TPACK framework should be introduced, explaining how the traditional TPACK model has been expanded to incorporate AI and how ethical dimensions have been integrated into it. The program may also include practical applications of AI-supported tools, such as personalized learning environments, automated feedback systems, and automated administrative tasks. Applied activities may include teachers designing lesson plans using AI-supported platforms for specific subject areas and conducting case studies analyzing the effectiveness of AI-supported assessment tools. Such a module has the potential to reduce teachers’ concerns about AI and enable them to integrate this technology effectively into their teaching processes.

The results that the relationship between teachers’ AI literacy and AI-TPACK is mediated by innovative thinking and moderated by AI anxiety underscore the necessity of concrete measures in teacher education, curriculum design, and AI- related policy development. Considering the association between teachers’ AI literacy and their propensity for innovative thinking, educational curricula must be restructured within the AI-TPACK framework. Curriculum developers should conceptualize artificial intelligence not merely as an auxiliary tool but as an integral component of the educational process, embedded across all learning objectives. Furthermore, curricula should be designed to enable teachers to discern AI tools that align with pedagogical goals and to enhance instructional practices accordingly. In addition, curricular frameworks must be flexible enough to address critical ethical dimensions, including algorithmic bias, data privacy, equitable access, and the sociotechnical implications of AI-driven decision-making processes. The mediating role of innovative thinking between AI literacy and AI-TPACK suggests that curricula should actively support cognitive processes that foster the generation and implementation of novel ideas.

Training and environments should be provided to develop teachers’ innovative thinking skills. Such approaches allow educators to develop creative and effective teaching strategies using new technologies such as AI. Strategies and support mechanisms to reduce teachers’ anxiety towards AI should be established. This may include providing accurate information about AI, offering opportunities for practical experience, and supporting groups or counseling services that address concerns. Both teacher training programs and in-service professional development can include modules that go beyond the technical use of AI tools and enable teachers to develop creative, transformative pedagogical approaches with AI. Educational policymakers and institutions should provide teachers with the necessary resources (technology, time, training) to develop their AI competencies. Schools should create areas where teachers can test AI tools and new teaching methodologies. Therefore, the establishment of physical or virtual environments such as “innovation laboratories” or “maker spaces” where innovative ideas can be implemented should be encouraged. These spaces can facilitate the practical application of innovative thinking. Given the widespread use of artificial intelligence in education, schools and education systems need to support teachers in adapting to the digital age.

## 5. Conclusion

The current study indicated complex interactions among AI literacy, AI-TPACK, innovative thinking, and AI anxiety. The results indicated that innovative thinking significantly mediates the relationship between AI literacy and AI-TPACK. Additionally, as teachers’ concerns about artificial intelligence decrease, the positive link between AI literacy and AI- TPACK strengthens further. These results suggest that developing innovative thinking and reducing concerns about AI can contribute to teachers’ more effective use of AI in their teaching. This study highlights the necessity of holistic approaches to ensure sustainable teacher adaptation to AI in the digital age. Importantly, these findings fill the initial gap by examining AI literacy, AI-TPACK, innovative thinking, and AI anxiety together within a single conditional process (moderated mediation) model. By demonstrating that innovative thinking mediates the effect of AI literacy on AI-TPACK while AI anxiety influences the strength of this relationship, the study offers a comprehensive view of the cognitive and emotional factors that influence teachers’ AI integration skills.
